text:
Artificial intelligence is significantly influencing universities and other higher education institutions. It is changing teaching, research, administration, and student support. While AI can increase efficiency and expand access to knowledge, universities must also reconsider assessment, academic standards, and the purpose of higher education.

In teaching, AI can support students by explaining difficult concepts, summarising readings, and generating practice questions. It may be particularly useful in large introductory courses where individual support is limited. Universities can also use AI systems to provide academic advising, answer administrative questions, and identify students at risk of dropping out.

AI is also transforming research. Researchers can use computational tools to analyse large datasets, review literature, translate documents, and identify patterns that would be difficult to detect manually. These capabilities may accelerate discovery across disciplines. However, researchers remain responsible for verifying results, acknowledging AI assistance, and protecting confidential information.

A major challenge concerns assessment. Traditional essays and take-home assignments may no longer demonstrate independent student ability when generative AI can produce complete responses. Universities may need to introduce oral examinations, supervised writing, practical projects, and reflective accounts of the research process.

AI also raises questions about graduate skills. Students must learn not only how to use AI but also how to evaluate its limitations. Employers may expect graduates to work effectively with automated systems while still demonstrating independent reasoning, ethical awareness, and professional judgement.

AI will not make universities unnecessary, but it will require them to redefine their educational role. Higher education must move beyond the simple delivery of information and focus more strongly on judgement, inquiry, collaboration, and responsible knowledge creation.
